claim_supported: pp.773-774 name exactly three sources of multiplicity: multiple outcomes, subgroups defined by observed characteristics, and multiple treatments. p.774 supplies the arithmetic that makes the gate default-on rather than discretionary: with independent tests at the five per cent level the probability of at least one false rejection is 0.226 at five hypotheses, 0.401 at ten and 0.994 at a hundred, and the same page reports that 84 per cent of the surveyed experiments examine five or more outcomes and 61 per cent ten or more. Remark 3.2 at p.779 is the decisive operational statement: Bonferroni and Holm are the same stepwise algorithm run with a fixed critical value that assumes a least favourable dependence structure, and the resampling procedure will always reject at least as many null hypotheses as they do. p.780 defines the adjusted p-value as the smallest level at which the hypothesis is rejected and recommends studentising. The applied section shows adjustment changing conclusions rather than decorating them: dollars given not including the match falls from significant at five per cent to significant only at ten (Table 1, p.782); two of four subgroups fall to one (Table 2, p.783); the 2:1 match moves from 0.0477 to 0.1297 and stops being significant at any conventional level (p.783, Table 3 p.784); and across the combined family of 48 hypotheses the rejections at ten per cent fall from 21 to 9, with 7 of the 9 attached to a single outcome (p.785). p.785 states the reporting standard the skill adopts, that multiplicity-adjusted results be reported alongside the conventional unadjusted ones

Remark 2.1 at p.777 assumes treatment status is i.i.d., so the procedure does not accommodate covariate-adaptive or stratified assignment designed to balance baseline covariates, and a design of that kind must be resolved before this source is cited. Assumption 2.3 at p.777 requires treatment and the subgroup variable to be discrete with finite support, so continuous moderators fall outside it. chapter_section: introduction and Testing for Equivalence (pp.355-356); Equivalence Tests for Differences Between Two Independent Means (pp.356-358) with Table 1 sample sizes (p.358); Setting Equivalence Bounds (pp.359-360); Discussion (pp.360-361)
page_or_article_locator: Soc Psychol Personal Sci 8(4):355-362; the four possible outcomes and Figure 1 at p.356; sample-size cost in Table 1 at p.358; the resource-determined bound and its worked numbers at p.359; operationalisation and competence limits at p.360
transfer_scope: concluding the absence of a meaningful effect, given a pre-specified bound
claim_supported: p.355 draws the distinction the rule rests on: it is statistically impossible to support the hypothesis that a true effect is exactly zero, but it is possible to reject effects large enough to be worthwhile, which is what the two one-sided tests procedure does against bounds set from the smallest effect size of interest. The same page documents how common the error is, with the phrase no effect appearing in 108 articles in one journal up to August 2016 almost always on the basis of nonsignificance, and Finch and colleagues reporting that around 38 per cent of articles with nonsignificant results in one applied journal accept the null. p.356 supplies the outcome table the skill now uses: with both a significance test and an equivalence test there are four results, not two, since an effect can be equivalent and not different, different and not equivalent, both different and equivalent, or undetermined, and the last of these is the honest verdict when the data settle nothing. The same page notes the 90 per cent interval is the right one because two one-sided tests are run at 5 per cent each. p.359 gives the bound-setting rule for the common case where theory fixes no boundary: set the bound to the smallest effect the available resources give sufficient power to detect, so that the maximum sample size one is willing to collect implicitly determines the smallest effect size of interest; with 100 per condition at 80 per cent power and alpha .05 that is about 0.414 for the equivalence test. p.358 prices the alternative, with a bound of d = 0.1 needing 1,713 per group at 80 per cent power against 191 at d = 0.3. p.359 also requires that when equivalence is claimed in an abstract, the bounds used be stated there too
claim_not_supported: that equivalence means an effect is absent, or absent for anyone. p.359 is explicit that bounds set from a researcher's own resources do not license a conclusion that the effect is too small to matter to others, who may reasonably fund a larger study. p.360 adds three further limits the rule now carries: the conclusion holds for the specific operationalisation tested and a different manipulation or measure may still show an effect; confounds can produce apparent equivalence; and whether the experiment was performed competently is a non-statistical question that no equivalence test settles, which the paper describes as an inherent asymmetry between showing an effect and showing the absence of a worthwhile one, resolvable only by independent replication. Nothing here supplies an economic minimum, which remains the analyst's burden under EMP-THRESH02

page_or_article_locator: J R Stat Soc B 57(1):289-300; FDR definition and its two properties at p.291; the three example types including screening at p.292; Theorem 1 and its independence condition at p.293; the mortality example at p.295; weak FWER control restated at p.298
transfer_scope: large exploratory families where the expected proportion of false rejections is the quantity of interest
claim_supported: p.291 defines the false discovery rate as the expected proportion of erroneous rejections among the rejected hypotheses and establishes the two properties that place it in the skill's hierarchy: when every null is true the FDR coincides with the familywise rate, so controlling FDR gives familywise control only in the weak sense, and when some nulls are false the FDR is no larger than the familywise rate, so any procedure controlling FWER already controls FDR while the converse buys power. p.290 states when the weaker criterion is appropriate, namely when a treatment and a control are compared on several aspects of one effect and the overall conclusion need not be wrong even if some individual nulls are falsely rejected. p.292 names the screening case directly, where many candidate effects are sifted and the concern is that too large a fraction of false leads would burden a second, confirmatory phase, which is exactly the skill's discovery family. p.293 gives the step-up procedure and Theorem 1. p.295 shows the stake concretely: among 15 comparisons Bonferroni and Hochberg each reject the same three and none is mortality, while the FDR procedure at q* = .05 rejects four including mortality at p = .0095 against a threshold of .013
claim_not_supported: validity under dependence, and confirmatory use. Theorem 1 at p.293 is proved for independent test statistics; the remark there relaxes independence only for the statistics attached to the false nulls, so a dependent family is outside what this paper establishes and the analyst must justify the dependence structure separately under CORE-M01. The 1995 paper contains no dependence-robust variant. p.291 and p.298 also make clear that FDR control delivers familywise control only weakly, so a rejection surviving this procedure does not discharge the strong familywise requirement a confirmatory claim carries and stays EXPLORATORY under this rule
